summary: Describes a pair of IP options for learning the smallest MTU, the largest packet size, along a path through an internet, and how that knowledge could be used. It was a proposal for an experimental protocol, and was replaced by RFC 1191.

eli5.summary: Before driving a truck, you want to know the narrowest tunnel on the route. These options let a sender find the biggest packet that fits the whole path.

questions: how do ip mtu discovery options work
what is the probe mtu option
subtitle: Two IP options to learn the smallest packet size that fits a network path.

tldr.problem: Fragmentation of packets causes poor performance and communication failures. Senders need to know the smallest maximum transmission unit (MTU) along their path to avoid fragmentation.
tldr.mechanism: Two IP options (Probe MTU and Reply MTU) let senders discover the minimum MTU by attaching them to packets; gateways and hosts update or return the lowest value they encounter.
tldr.outcome: This experimental approach was superseded by RFC 1191, which uses a different strategy based on ICMP feedback.

today: RFC 1063 was an experimental approach to path MTU discovery. It was superseded by RFC 1191, which became the standard for this function. The Probe/Reply option approach was not widely deployed.

sections.title: The Fragmentation Problem
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol allows gateways to break up (fragment) packets that are too large to forward. However, fragmentation is undesirable because it causes poor performance and sometimes complete communication failure. A datagram gets fragmented whenever it is larger than the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of some network along its path. To avoid fragmentation, a sending host must know the smallest MTU across the entire path, called the Minimum MTU or MINMTU.

At the time RFC 1063 was written, finding the MINMTU was difficult. Senders either had to use conservatively small packets (wasting bandwidth) or send probe packets to discover when fragmentation occurs (adding network overhead). These approaches fail to detect when paths change, which often happens in real networks.
sections.eli5: Big packets get broken into pieces if they hit a narrow part of the network. You want to know how big is the narrowest part so you can send the right size from the start.

sections.title: The Two IP Options
sections.content:
RFC 1063 proposes two new IP options to solve this problem. The Probe MTU option (number 11) is a 4-byte header that carries the lowest MTU value seen so far on the path. A sending host initializes it with its own network's MTU. As the packet travels, each gateway and host examines the option and, if their network is narrower than the value in the option, they reduce it. The Reply MTU option (number 12) is identical in structure but serves a different purpose: it carries the learned MINMTU back to the sender in a return packet.

Both options have the same format: a 1-byte type field, a 1-byte length field (4), and a 2-byte value field containing the MTU in octets. The format allows for straightforward parsing and updating by IP layers and gateways.
sections.eli5: One option holds a number representing the narrowest part found so far. Every stop along the way checks if it is narrower and updates the number. The other option sends that number back to the sender.

sections.title: How Discovery Works
sections.content:
The RFC describes two implementation approaches. In the transport-layer approach, the transport protocol (such as TCP) includes the Probe MTU option in outgoing datagrams and the receiving transport layer responds with a Reply MTU option. In the IP-layer approach, which is recommended, the IP layer manages discovery automatically using information stored in the routing cache. When the IP layer sends a packet, it checks whether a probe needs to be sent to the destination; if so, it adds the Probe MTU option. When a probe option arrives, the receiving IP layer stores that value and sends a Reply MTU option in the next outgoing packet to the sender.

The scheme requires careful handling of multiple factors: the sender should not send probes continuously but approximately once per round-trip time, hosts should stop probing if the destination does not support the option after several attempts, and implementations should not probe broadcast addresses. When a reply arrives, the sender compares the returned MTU against its current estimate; if lower, it updates immediately; if higher, it waits for the estimate to age before accepting the increase to avoid flapping.
sections.eli5: You send a special packet asking 'how big is the narrowest part to you?' Each stop updates it. When someone sends you a message, they include the answer. You remember the smallest number you ever got.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC provides detailed guidance for IP-layer implementations. The routing cache should store seven additional values for each destination: the current MINMTU estimate, when the next probe should be sent, when the MTU was last decreased, whether a reply option should be included in the next outgoing packet, the value to go in that reply, whether the remote peer supports probing, and how many consecutive probes have been sent without a response.

Implementors must also handle an interaction with the TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option. Because the MSS assumes no IP options, adding MTU options can violate the negotiated MSS. The RFC suggests either reserving 4 bytes from the reported MINMTU (simple but wasteful) or coordinating with the transport layer when options will be added (complex but more efficient).
sections.eli5: Keeping track of the path MTU is complicated. You have to remember when you last heard about it, when you asked, and whether the other end even understands these options. You also need to leave room for the option itself in the packet.

sections.title: Status and Replacement
sections.content: RFC 1063 was published as an experimental protocol. It was not widely adopted and was superseded by RFC 1191, which specifies a Path MTU Discovery mechanism that uses a different approach: instead of requiring IP options in every packet, it relies on ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages from gateways. When a gateway encounters a packet too large to forward without fragmentation, it sends an ICMP message to the source telling it the MTU of the offending link. This approach requires no changes to IP headers and scales better than the Probe/Reply option scheme.
sections.eli5: This idea of using special options in every packet turned out not to work well. A better idea came along: when someone sends a packet that is too big, the network tells them by sending an error message back. This became the standard way.
